> Interoceptive perception—the conscious awareness and interpretation of internal bodily signals—also plays a significant role in anxiety, with evidence showing that both heightened and reduced interoceptive awareness can contribute to anxious states (Zoltowski et al., 2024; Clemente et al., 2024; Kiera et al., 2025; Ironside et al., 2023). #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety  #perception/interoception

# \#trust (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> Neuroception refers to the brain’s automatic detection of safety or threat without conscious awareness. It is central to Polyvagal Theory and underlies rapid autonomic responses that initiate anxiety before conscious processing occurs (Paulus & Stein, 2010; Harrison et al., 2021). #threat/unconcious_processing #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety #models/polyvagal #perception/neuroception 
> Neuroceptive processes are especially relevant for social trust/distrust judgments—subtle cues can trigger physiological arousal or calmness **even when not consciously perceived** ([[#^782b79|Paulus & Stein, 2010]]). Altered neuroceptive signaling is implicated in heightened threat sensitivity seen in anxiety disorders ([[#^2a1a85|Harrison et al., 2021]]). #trust #cognitive/anxiety/trait_anxiety #perception/neuroception #threat/unconcious_processing  ^f55d2c ^tr-x4m4i8etn

# \#cognitive/anxiety (2)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> ==Interoceptive perception involves detecting and interpreting internal bodily signals (e.g., heartbeat, breathing).== Research shows complex links between interoceptive confusion/accuracy and anxiety: both **hyperawareness** (over-attention) and **hypoawareness** (reduced detection) can maintain or exacerbate anxious states ([[#^b5c11f|Zoltowski et al., 2024]]; [[#^b1948b|Clemente et al., 2024]]; [[#^6dc23e|Kiera et al., 2025]]; [[#^a98b36|Ironside et al., 2023]]). #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety #perception/interoception #perception/interoception/definition #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety/hyperawareness #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety/hypoawareness
> Negative evaluation or misinterpretation of bodily signals perpetuates anxiety ([[#^b1948b|Clemente et al., 2024]]; [[#^6dc23e|Kiera et al., 2025]]), while interventions targeting interoceptive skills can reduce it ([[#^a98e9f|Adams et al., 2022]]). #cognitive/anxiety #perception/interoception ^tr-qo9m0wk6j

> > The relationship between **anxiety** and **motor control** can be explained through established theoretical frameworks. According to **execution focus models**, anxiety increases **mental effort** and **conscious movement monitoring**, which disrupts automatic control processes (Beilock and Carr, 2001; Nieuwenhuys and Oudejans, 2012). 
> > The constrained action hypothesis further suggests that **anxiety-induced internal focus** impairs the unconscious, reflexive control processes that normally regulate coordinated movement (Wulf et al., 2001). 
> > *These theoretical perspectives suggest that sensorimotor mismatch-induced anxiety can lower automaticity.*

# \#perception/safety/factors/human_factors/sense_of_ownership (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> This is catastrophic for wearable robots because proprioception acts as the sensory mediator for the "Sense of Agency"—without precise proprioceptive feedback, the user cannot achieve the psychological state of "human-in-the-loop" trust ([[Why Anxiety?#Embodiment and Proprioception]]). Proprioception is richly represented in the somatosensory cortex, especially S1, where it is integrated with touch and used to update internal body representations (Why Anxiety?, [[Somatosensory Cortices]], #somatosensory_cortex). When anxiety disrupts this integration, embodiment—the sense of ownership and agency critical for natural movement, intuitive control, and effective rehabilitation—becomes impossible (Target word 'cognitive or perception', 1 Embodiment Drives Functional Success, #perception/safety/factors/human_factors/sense_of_agency, #perception/safety/factors/human_factors/sense_of_ownership). ^tr-r3ipyd9pr

> [!info]+ 2
> - Measuring perceived risk in human-robot interaction (HRI) involves capturing individuals' subjective judgments about potential harm or safety related to robots. 
> - While no HRI-specific perceived risk scale is directly described in the available research, related constructs such as **perceived safety** and **risk perception** have been measured using validated questionnaires and multidimensional scales. 
> ###perception/risk
> ###perception/safety
> - For example, standardized measurement tools for perceived safety in robots have been developed alongside assessments of anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, and perceived intelligence, using semantic differential scales to ensure **reliability** and **validity**  ([[#^d9c7d4|Bartneck et al., 2009]]). 
> - More broadly, perceived risk is often conceptualized as a multidimensional construct including factors like **exposure**, **susceptibility**, **severity**, and **affective response**, with empirically supported subscales developed to measure these dimensions across different hazard contexts  ([[#^381ae7|Walpole & Wilson, 2021]]; [[#^1f3fde|Wilson et al., 2018]]). 
> - *These approaches emphasize the importance of **affective reactions** and **perceived severity**, which could be adapted to HRI contexts to assess how users perceive risk from robots.* 
> - Additionally, careful item wording and **awareness of biases** are crucial for accurate measurement, as **risk perception can be influenced by heuristics and subjective interpretations**  ([[#^a0c342|Wolff et al., 2019]]).

# \#threat (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> 
> - Finely tuned motor control breaks down most commonly due to negative emotional state of anxiety. #cognitive/anxiety 
> - What we perceive from the world, is not what it actually is, but the brain's best guess based on a trade-off between the prior probability and the hypothesis that fits the current sensory input. #perception 
> - Our brains select hypotheses in a Bayes-optimal manner, based on how well those hypotheses minimize prediction error. #baysian #prediction_error  ^de0b99
> - In perceptual inference, prediction errors are minimized by the organism updating their model of the world to fit input. #perception/perceptual_inference ^pe
> - In active inference, the prediction is generated and then the (predicted) state of affairs is brought about as part of the prediction error minimisation imperative. #threat #predictive_processing #cognitive/anxiety/hypervigilance  #chemicals/neurotransmitters/Norepinephrine  #neuroscience/active_inrefence_theory ^tr-omd0zzonh
>

# \#perception/safety/human_factors/traits/personality (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> 
> ###### Findings on Human Characteristics and Perceived Safety
> - **Personality** significantly impacts perceived safety; specifically, individuals with low **neuroticism** experience higher perceived safety and sense of control, as neuroticism relates to a tendency for negative emotions and **anxiety**.
> - **Extraversion** correlates with higher arousal during interaction but not directly with perceived safety; 
> - **Conscientiousness** shows moderate positive correlation with positive emotional valence.

# \#perception/safety/factors/human_factors/sense_of_control (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> - The study employed physiological signals (**EDA**, **heart rate variability**) collected via **wristbands** and **facial affect analysis** from video recordings **alongside questionnaires** to evaluate perceived safety. #measures/objective_measures 
> - **Physiological data provided higher accuracy in predicting perceived safety** (up to 79% accuracy) compared to facial affect data, indicating stronger promise for objective monitoring of safety perception. #perception/safety 
> ^p-safety-measure
> - **Positive emotional valence** correlates with higher perceived safety, though discrete emotions like **anger** and **fear** did not show correlation in this study. #cognitive/fear #cognitive/anger
> ###### Additional Observations and Emerging Factors
> - **inadequate transparency** during **unpredictable** or **failed** robot behaviors. #trust_factors/robot_factors/transparency #perception/safety/factors/robot_factors/transparency  ^58f94b
> - a perceived **need to regain control** in unsafe scenarios. #perception/safety/factors/human_factors/sense_of_control ^462db9 ^tr-td58ohve2

# \#Time (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> 
> ###  Time perception [Link](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/psychology/time-perception#full-article) 
> ###Time #perception/time
> - The way the brain processes information is also believed to have an effect on time perception. When the brain receives raw information from the senses, it does not process that information in the correct order. The brain needs time to reorganize that information in such a way that it can be interpreted and understood. 
> - As would be expected, the brain takes longer to recognize [[new]] information and less time to process familiar information. Because the information from [[new]] experiences requires extra processing time, those moments can seem to last longer, while familiar experiences seem shorter. ^tr-erpyq9yvu
